modules.title: 1 · Why a linear model fails for 0/1 outcomes
modules.summary: When y is 0 or 1, fitting a straight line (the Linear Probability Model) breaks down: it predicts probabilities outside [0,1], has built-in heteroskedasticity, and imposes a constant effect that cannot be globally true.

stages.title: Binary outcomes and the urge to run OLS
stages.html:
Modelling a yes/no outcome

Many outcomes are binary: a loan defaults or not, a patient recovers or not, a customer buys or not. We code these as y ∈ {0,1}. The natural quantity of interest is the probability that y = 1 given some features x:

p(x) = P(y = 1 | x)

A tempting first move is to just run OLS of y on x. That is called the Linear Probability Model (LPM):

P(y = 1 | x) = β₀ + β₁·x₁ + β₂·x₂ + …

It is fast, the coefficients read directly as "a one-unit rise in x changes the probability by β", and for x near the data centre it is often a decent approximation. But it has three structural problems that get worse near the edges.

Key idea. A probability must live in [0,1] and the way x moves it cannot be a straight line forever — eventually the line must bend, or it will predict nonsense.

stages.title: Three things that go wrong
stages.html:
1. Predictions escape [0,1]

A line has no ceiling or floor. Push x far enough and ŷ goes below 0 or above 1 — an impossible probability. You cannot interpret "there is a 130% chance of default."

2. The errors are heteroskedastic by construction

If y is Bernoulli with success probability p, its variance is p·(1−p). That depends on x, so the OLS homoskedasticity assumption is automatically violated and the default standard errors are wrong.

3. A constant marginal effect is implausible

LPM says one extra unit of x always changes the probability by the same β. But moving someone from a 50% chance to 60% is easy, while moving them from 98% to 100% should be nearly impossible. The real effect of x must shrink near 0 and 1.

Key idea. We want an S-shaped curve that is squeezed into (0,1): steep in the middle, flat at the extremes. That is exactly what logit and probit deliver.

stages.title: Watch the LPM predict impossible probabilities
stages.note: We simulate a true logistic process, fit OLS (the LPM), and print how many fitted 'probabilities' fall outside [0,1]. The scatter shows the flat line cutting through 0 and 1.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600
x = rng.normal(0, 1.6, n)
eta = -0.4 + 2.2*x            # true log-odds
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta))        # true probability
y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x': x})

lpm = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit()
phat = lpm.predict(df)
out = ((phat < 0) | (phat > 1)).sum()
print('LPM fitted prob range: [%.3f, %.3f]' % (phat.min(), phat.max()))
print('Fitted values outside [0,1]: %d of %d (%.1f%%)' % (out, n, 100*out/n))

xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(x, y, s=10, color='#da9100', alpha=.35, label='data (0/1)')
plt.plot(xs, lpm.params['Intercept']+lpm.params['x']*xs, color='#6f6b57', lw=2, label='LPM line')
plt.axhline(0, color='#c9c6ac', lw=1); plt.axhline(1, color='#c9c6ac', lw=1)
plt.ylim(-0.4, 1.4); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y / predicted prob')
plt.title('LPM: %d impossible predictions outside [0,1]' % out)
plt.legend(loc='best', fontsize=8)

stages.title: How far out of bounds does the line go?
stages.note: Increase the true slope or shift the intercept. The steeper and more off-centre the relationship, the further the straight LPM line pokes past 0 and 1. The title reports how many fitted probabilities are impossible.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
x = rng.normal(0, 1.6, n)
eta = {{intercept}} + {{slope}}*x
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta))
y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x': x})
lpm = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit()
phat = lpm.predict(df)
out = int(((phat < 0) | (phat > 1)).sum())
xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(x, y, s=10, color='#da9100', alpha=.3)
plt.plot(xs, lpm.params['Intercept']+lpm.params['x']*xs, color='#6f6b57', lw=2)
plt.axhline(0, color='#c9c6ac', lw=1); plt.axhline(1, color='#c9c6ac', lw=1)
plt.ylim(-0.5, 1.5); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('predicted prob')
plt.title('LPM impossible predictions: %d of %d' % (out, n))

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Which problem is NOT a structural flaw of the Linear Probability Model for a 0/1 outcome?
choices: Fitted probabilities can fall below 0 or above 1
The error variance p(1−p) depends on x, so errors are heteroskedastic
It forces a constant marginal effect of x at every probability level
It can only be estimated by maximum likelihood, never by OLS
stages.hint: Think about how the LPM is actually fit versus what logit/probit require.
stages.explain: The LPM is fit by ordinary least squares — that is its whole appeal. The genuine flaws are out-of-range predictions, built-in heteroskedasticity, and a constant (rather than diminishing) marginal effect.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Why should the effect of x on P(y=1) shrink as the probability approaches 0 or 1?
choices: Because the sample size falls at the extremes
Because a probability is bounded in [0,1], so there is little room left to move
Because OLS standard errors grow at the extremes
Because x stops varying at the extremes
stages.hint: You cannot push a probability above 1.
stages.explain: Near the floor or ceiling there is almost no room left, so the same change in x can only nudge the probability a tiny amount — implying an S-shaped curve, not a straight line.

stages.title: Does a straight line have a constant effect?
stages.prompt: You just saw the Linear Probability Model fit a straight line to a 0/1 outcome. Claim: because the line is straight, a one-unit rise in x changes P(y=1) by the same amount whether you start at p=0.05 or at p=0.95.
stages.hint: A straight line has one slope everywhere — that is the whole point of the module. Is that constant effect realistic near the 0 and 1 boundaries?
stages.explain: This is the constant-marginal-effect flaw of the LPM. The claim is literally TRUE of the straight line — its slope is the same everywhere — and that is exactly why the LPM is wrong for probabilities: near p=0.95 there is almost no room left to move, so a real effect must shrink at the extremes. The fix is an S-curve (logit/probit) whose slope flattens in the tails. Boundary: a constant effect is only defensible over a narrow middle range where the fitted probabilities stay far from 0 and 1.

modules.title: 2 · The logit (and probit) model
modules.summary: Logit and probit pass a linear index β₀+β₁x through an S-shaped link (the logistic CDF or the standard-normal CDF) to keep probabilities in (0,1). Both are fit by maximum likelihood; their coefficients differ only by a roughly constant scale factor.

stages.title: Squash the line through an S-curve
stages.html:
From a line to a probability

Keep the familiar linear part — call it the linear index or log-odds:

η = β₀ + β₁·x₁ + β₂·x₂ + …

η ranges over the whole real line, from −∞ to +∞. To turn it into a probability we feed it through a smooth, increasing function that maps (−∞, +∞) into (0,1). For logit that function is the logistic (a.k.a. sigmoid):

p = Λ(η) = 1 / (1 + e^(−η))

For probit it is the standard-normal CDF Φ:

p = Φ(η)

Both are S-shaped: near η = 0 they pass through p = 0.5 and rise steeply; as η → ±∞ they flatten against 1 and 0. The probability can never escape the unit interval — problem #1 from Module 1 is solved automatically.

Key idea. Same linear index, different S-shaped link. Logit uses the logistic CDF; probit uses the normal CDF.

stages.title: The logit's special trick: log-odds are linear
stages.html:
Odds and log-odds

The odds of success are p / (1 − p) — e.g. p = 0.8 means odds of 4-to-1. Invert the logistic and something elegant pops out:

log( p / (1 − p) ) = β₀ + β₁·x₁ + …

So in the logit model the log-odds are exactly linear in x. That is why β₁ has a clean meaning: a one-unit rise in x₁ adds β₁ to the log-odds, i.e. multiplies the odds by e^(β₁). (We exploit this in Module 3.)

How are they fit?

There is no closed-form least-squares solution. Instead we choose the β's that make the observed 0/1 pattern most probable — maximum likelihood (MLE). statsmodels does this for you: smf.logit(...).fit() and smf.probit(...).fit(). The output reports z-statistics (not t), a Log-Likelihood, and a Pseudo R² instead of the usual R².

Key idea. Logit makes the log-odds linear in x; probit makes a normal z-score linear in x. Both are estimated by maximum likelihood.

stages.title: Fit logit, recover the truth, and compare to probit
stages.note: We simulate from a known logistic process (intercept −0.3, slopes +1.5 and −0.8), fit logit by MLE, and confirm the estimates land near the truth. Then we fit probit on the same data and show the coefficients differ by a near-constant scale (~1.6–1.8), even though the fitted probabilities almost coincide.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n); x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eta = -0.3 + 1.5*x1 - 0.8*x2          # true log-odds
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta))
y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x1': x1, 'x2': x2})

logit = smf.logit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)
probit = smf.probit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)
print(logit.summary())
print('\nTrue coefs:      const=-0.30  x1= 1.50  x2=-0.80')
print('Logit  estimates:', np.round(logit.params.values, 3))
print('Probit estimates:', np.round(probit.params.values, 3))
print('Logit/Probit ratio (x1, x2):',
      np.round((logit.params[['x1','x2']]/probit.params[['x1','x2']]).values, 3))
ph_l = logit.predict(df); ph_p = probit.predict(df)
print('Max abs gap between logit & probit fitted probs: %.4f' % (np.abs(ph_l-ph_p).max()))

stages.title: Shape the S-curve by hand
stages.note: Move the index intercept β₀ and slope β₁ and watch the logistic curve P(y=1)=1/(1+e^-(β₀+β₁x)). The curve crosses 0.5 where the index is zero (x = −β₀/β₁), and its steepest slope equals β₁/4. Bigger |β₁| = sharper S.
stages.template:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm
xs = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
log_p = 1/(1+np.exp(-({{b0}}+{{b1}}*xs)))
prob_p = norm.cdf({{b0}}+{{b1}}*xs)
b1 = {{b1}}
x50 = (-{{b0}}/b1) if abs(b1) > 1e-9 else float('nan')
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(xs, log_p, color='#da9100', lw=2.4, label='logit (logistic)')
plt.plot(xs, prob_p, color='#af983f', lw=1.6, ls='--', label='probit (normal)')
plt.axhline(0.5, color='#6f6b57', lw=1, ls=':')
plt.ylim(-0.03, 1.03); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('P(y=1)')
plt.title('crosses 0.5 at x=%.2f   max slope (logit)=%.3f' % (x50, b1/4))
plt.legend(loc='lower right', fontsize=8)

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: In a logit model, a one-unit increase in x₁ (holding others fixed) does exactly what?
choices: Adds β₁ to the probability P(y=1)
Adds β₁ to the log-odds of y=1
Multiplies the probability by β₁
Adds β₁ to the normal z-score Φ⁻¹(p)
stages.hint: What is the inverse of the logistic link?
stages.explain: The logit link makes log[p/(1−p)] = β₀+β₁x linear, so a unit rise in x₁ adds exactly β₁ to the log-odds (adding β₁ to the normal z-score is the probit statement, not logit).

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: You fit the same data with logit and probit. What do you expect?
choices: Identical coefficients and identical fitted probabilities
Very different fitted probabilities but identical coefficients
Coefficients differing by a roughly constant scale, with nearly identical fitted probabilities
Probit coefficients exactly double the logit coefficients
stages.hint: The logistic and normal CDFs have different variances but similar S-shapes.
stages.explain: Because the logistic and normal links have different scales, logit coefficients run about 1.6–1.8 times the probit ones, yet the predicted probabilities and overall fit are almost indistinguishable.

stages.title: Is the coefficient a probability change?
stages.prompt: You just fit the logit and read β̂₁ off the summary, with log[p/(1−p)] = β₀ + β₁x. Claim: β̂₁ is the change in the probability P(y=1) for a one-unit rise in x.
stages.hint: Look at what the link makes linear. β multiplies x on the log-odds scale, not on the probability scale.
stages.explain: This is the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap, the central logit error. β is a constant change in the log-odds, not the probability: log[p/(1−p)] = β₀+β₁x is what's linear in x. The effect on the probability is β·p(1−p) — non-linear, largest near p=0.5 and tiny in the tails — so it has no single value. Boundary: only on the log-odds scale is the effect a constant β; on the probability scale you must compute an (average) marginal effect.

stages.title: What does the logit make linear?
stages.prompt: The logit's special trick: it makes the ___ a linear function β₀+β₁x of the regressors.
stages.lead: The logistic link is chosen precisely because one transformation of the probability comes out linear in x — name that quantity.
stages.hint: It is the natural log of p/(1−p). Two words, hyphenated — or the one-word name of the link itself.
stages.explain: The logit (log-odds) is what comes out linear: log[p/(1−p)] = β₀+β₁x. Students often answer 'probability' or 'odds', but neither is linear in x — only the log of the odds is, which is exactly why β adds to the log-odds and not to p. Boundary: exponentiate once and you get the odds (multiplied by e^β); the probability itself is the non-linear S-curve and is never linear in x.

modules.title: 3 · Interpreting coefficients: odds ratios & marginal effects
modules.summary: A raw logit coefficient is a change in log-odds — not very intuitive. Exponentiate it to get an odds ratio (a multiplicative effect on the odds), or compute a marginal effect dP/dx (the change in probability), which is largest near p=0.5 and shrinks at the extremes.

stages.title: Three currencies for the same effect
stages.html:
Log-odds, odds, or probability?

The estimated β₁ is in log-odds units, which almost nobody thinks in. We translate it into two friendlier currencies.

Odds ratio: e^(β₁)

Because the log-odds are linear, exponentiating undoes the log:

odds-ratio = e^(β₁)

A one-unit rise in x₁ multiplies the odds by e^(β₁). If β₁ = 0.7 then e^(0.7) ≈ 2.0: the odds double. If e^(β₁) > 1 the feature raises the odds; if < 1 it lowers them; if = 1 it has no effect. This factor is constant everywhere — that is the elegance of the odds scale.

Marginal effect: dP/dx

People often want the effect on the probability, not the odds. For logit:

∂P/∂x₁ = β₁ · p · (1 − p)

This is not constant — it depends on where you are on the curve. It peaks at p = 0.5 (factor 0.25·β₁) and vanishes as p → 0 or 1. statsmodels averages it across the sample with res.get_margeff() (the Average Marginal Effect).

Key idea. Odds ratio = constant multiplicative effect on the odds. Marginal effect = change in probability, biggest in the middle of the S, smallest at the tails.

stages.title: Reading the numbers correctly
stages.html:
Pitfalls to avoid

  • Do not read the raw β as a probability change — it is a log-odds change.
  • An odds ratio of 2.0 does not mean the probability doubles. Going from 50% (odds 1) to odds 2 is 67%, not 100%.
  • The marginal effect needs a reference point. Average Marginal Effect (AME) computes dP/dx for every observation and averages — usually the most honest summary. Marginal Effect at the Means (MEM) plugs in the average x instead.
  • For a binary regressor, the cleaner summary is the discrete change in predicted probability from 0 to 1, not the derivative.

Rule of thumb for logit: divide a coefficient by 4 to get the maximum marginal effect on probability. β₁ = 1.5 → up to about 0.375 change in probability per unit of x, near p = 0.5.

Key idea. The 'divide-by-4' rule gives the steepest possible probability effect; the actual average marginal effect is usually smaller because most observations sit off the p=0.5 peak.

stages.title: Odds ratios and average marginal effects
stages.note: We fit logit, exponentiate the coefficients to read odds ratios, and call get_margeff() for the average marginal effects (the change in probability). Notice the AME for x1 is well below β1/4 — most observations are off the steepest part of the curve.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n); x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eta = -0.3 + 1.5*x1 - 0.8*x2
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta)); y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x1': x1, 'x2': x2})

res = smf.logit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)
odds = np.exp(res.params)
print('Coefficients (log-odds):')
print(np.round(res.params, 3).to_string())
print('\nOdds ratios  exp(coef):')
print(np.round(odds, 3).to_string())
print('\nInterpretation: +1 in x1 multiplies the odds by %.2f' % odds['x1'])
print('               +1 in x2 multiplies the odds by %.2f (i.e. lowers them)' % odds['x2'])
print('\ndivide-by-4 max marginal effect for x1: %.3f' % (res.params['x1']/4))
print('\n', res.get_margeff().summary())

stages.title: See the marginal effect change along the curve
stages.note: Pick a slope β₁ and a point x*. The orange dot is P(y=1) there; the dashed tangent is the local slope dP/dx = β₁·p·(1−p). Drag x* toward the tails and watch the tangent flatten even though β₁ never changes — that is why 'the' marginal effect is not a single number.
stages.template:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
b1 = {{b1}}; b0 = 0.0; xstar = {{xstar}}
xs = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
P = 1/(1+np.exp(-(b0+b1*xs)))
ps = 1/(1+np.exp(-(b0+b1*xstar)))
slope = b1*ps*(1-ps)            # dP/dx at x*
tang = ps + slope*(xs - xstar)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(xs, P, color='#da9100', lw=2.4)
plt.plot(xs, np.clip(tang,-0.1,1.1), color='#6f6b57', lw=1.5, ls='--')
plt.scatter([xstar],[ps], color='#af983f', zorder=5, s=40)
plt.ylim(-0.03,1.03); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('P(y=1)')
plt.title('at x*=%.1f:  P=%.3f   dP/dx=%.3f   (max=%.3f)' % (xstar, ps, slope, b1/4))

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: A logit gives a coefficient of 0.69 on x₁. What is the cleanest one-line interpretation?
choices: A one-unit rise in x₁ raises P(y=1) by 0.69
A one-unit rise in x₁ roughly doubles the odds of y=1, since e^0.69≈2
A one-unit rise in x₁ doubles the probability of y=1
x₁ explains 69% of the variation in y
stages.explain: e^0.69 ≈ 2, so the odds (not the probability) are multiplied by about 2 — the odds ratio is the constant, exponentiated read of a logit coefficient.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Why is the average marginal effect (dP/dx) usually smaller than coefficient/4?
choices: Because statsmodels uses robust standard errors
Because coefficient/4 is the maximum effect, reached only at p=0.5, and most observations sit away from there
Because marginal effects ignore the intercept
Because the AME is measured in odds, not probability
stages.hint: Where on the S-curve is p·(1−p) largest?
stages.explain: The factor p·(1−p) peaks at 0.25 when p=0.5, giving the divide-by-4 maximum; observations in the flatter tails contribute smaller slopes, pulling the average below that peak.

stages.title: Turn the coefficient into an odds ratio
stages.prompt: A logit gives a coefficient of 0.69 on treated. The odds ratio is exp(β). Enter exp(0.69) to two decimals (a plain number, no units).
stages.hint: exp(0.69) is just under 2. This multiplies the ODDS — it is not a change in probability.
stages.explain: exp(0.69) = 1.99 ≈ 2.00 — treatment roughly DOUBLES the odds. This is the odds-ratio reading of a logit coefficient, and it is constant across x. It is NOT a doubling of the probability and NOT the marginal effect on P(y=1): odds and probability move together only when p is small. Boundary: the odds ratio e^β is the one effect measure that does stay constant; the probability effect β·p(1−p) does not.

stages.title: The marginal effect at p = 0.5
stages.prompt: A logit gives β=0.8 on a binary treatment. At a baseline probability p=0.5, the marginal effect on P(y=1) is β·p(1−p). Enter it to two decimals (a probability change, e.g. 0.20).
stages.hint: Plug in: 0.8 × 0.5 × (1−0.5). The answer is a quarter of β here, not β itself.
stages.explain: This is the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap in numbers: the marginal effect is β·p(1−p) = 0.8·0.25 = 0.20, NOT the coefficient 0.8. And it shrinks toward the tails — at p=0.9 it is only 0.8·0.09 = 0.072. That p-dependence is exactly why you cannot read a logit coefficient as a single, constant change in probability. Boundary: p(1−p) peaks at 0.25 (p=0.5), so β/4 is the largest the marginal effect can ever be; everywhere else it is smaller.

stages.title: Reading a logit coefficient — select all
stages.prompt: A logit reports β=0.69 on treated. Select all that apply — which statements are correct readings of this coefficient?
choices: It adds 0.69 to the log-odds of y=1 for a one-unit change in treated
The odds of y=1 are multiplied by about 2 (e^0.69 ≈ 2)
It raises the probability P(y=1) by 0.69
It is the marginal effect dP/dx, the same at every value of x
The effect on probability depends on the baseline p, peaking near p=0.5
stages.hint: Two correct statements live on the log-odds/odds scale; one more is about how the probability effect varies. The two probability-as-constant statements are the trap.
stages.explain: Correct readings: β adds to the log-odds (0), the odds are multiplied by e^β ≈ 2 (1), and the probability effect varies with the baseline p, peaking near p=0.5 (4). The two distractors are the coefficient-is-a-marginal-effect trap: β is NOT a 0.69 jump in probability (2) and NOT a constant dP/dx (3) — the probability effect is β·p(1−p), which changes along the S-curve. Boundary: only the log-odds increment and the odds ratio e^β are constant; any probability statement must name the p at which it is evaluated.

modules.title: 4 · Model fit & classification
modules.summary: Judge a binary model by likelihood-based fit (pseudo-R², LR test) and by classification: turn predicted probabilities into 0/1 at a threshold, build a confusion matrix, read accuracy, and trace the threshold-free ROC curve and its AUC — all with numpy, no sklearn.

stages.title: Two ways to ask 'is it any good?'
stages.html:
Fit versus classification

There is no ordinary R² in MLE land. statsmodels reports McFadden's Pseudo R² = 1 − ℓ(model)/ℓ(null), comparing the fitted log-likelihood to a null model with only an intercept. Values of 0.2–0.4 already indicate a strong fit — do not expect the 0.9 you might see in OLS. The LLR p-value is a likelihood-ratio test that all slopes are jointly zero (the binary analogue of the overall F-test).

From probabilities to decisions

To actually classify, pick a threshold (commonly 0.5) and predict ŷ = 1 when p̂ ≥ threshold. Cross-tabulate against the truth to get the confusion matrix:

  • TP true positives, TN true negatives — correct calls.
  • FP false positives (predicted 1, actually 0), FN false negatives (predicted 0, actually 1) — the two error types.

accuracy = (TP + TN) / n

Key idea. Pseudo-R² and the LR test grade the probabilities; the confusion matrix and accuracy grade the 0/1 decisions at a chosen threshold.

stages.title: Why one threshold is not enough: ROC & AUC
stages.html:
Accuracy can lie

If 90% of cases are y = 0, a lazy model that always predicts 0 scores 90% accuracy while catching zero positives. With imbalance you need to look at both error types and to vary the threshold.

The ROC curve

Sweep the threshold from 1 down to 0. At each one record the true-positive rate TPR = TP/(all actual 1s) and the false-positive rate FPR = FP/(all actual 0s). Plotting TPR against FPR traces the ROC curve. A perfect model hugs the top-left corner; random guessing is the 45° diagonal.

The area under that curve, the AUC, summarises ranking quality in one number: it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher p̂ than a randomly chosen negative. AUC = 0.5 is coin-flipping; AUC = 1.0 is perfect separation; 0.8+ is generally strong. AUC is threshold-free, so it judges the probabilities themselves rather than one cut-off.

Key idea. AUC measures how well the model ranks positives above negatives, independent of any threshold — robust even when classes are imbalanced.

stages.title: Confusion matrix, accuracy, and a hand-rolled ROC/AUC
stages.note: Pure numpy: threshold predicted probabilities at 0.5 for the confusion matrix and accuracy, then sweep all thresholds to build the ROC curve and integrate it with the trapezoid rule (no sklearn, no np.trapz).
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n); x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eta = -0.3 + 1.5*x1 - 0.8*x2
p = 1/(1+np.exp(-eta)); y = rng.binomial(1, p)
df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y, 'x1': x1, 'x2': x2})
res = smf.logit('y ~ x1 + x2', df).fit(disp=0)

y = df['y'].to_numpy()
phat = res.predict(df).to_numpy()
yhat = (phat >= 0.5).astype(int)
TP = int(((yhat==1)&(y==1)).sum()); TN = int(((yhat==0)&(y==0)).sum())
FP = int(((yhat==1)&(y==0)).sum()); FN = int(((yhat==0)&(y==1)).sum())
acc = (TP+TN)/n
print('Pseudo R-squared: %.3f' % res.prsquared)
print('Confusion matrix (rows=actual, cols=predicted):')
print('            pred 0   pred 1')
print('actual 0   %6d   %6d' % (TN, FP))
print('actual 1   %6d   %6d' % (FN, TP))
print('Accuracy @0.5: %.3f' % acc)

P = (y==1).sum(); N = (y==0).sum()
thr = np.linspace(0, 1, 201)
tpr = np.array([((phat>=t)&(y==1)).sum()/P for t in thr])
fpr = np.array([((phat>=t)&(y==0)).sum()/N for t in thr])
order = np.argsort(fpr); fs = fpr[order]; ts = tpr[order]
auc = float(np.sum((fs[1:]-fs[:-1])*(ts[1:]+ts[:-1])/2))   # trapezoid
print('AUC: %.3f' % auc)

plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color='#da9100', lw=2.2, label='ROC (AUC=%.3f)' % auc)
plt.plot([0,1],[0,1], color='#6f6b57', lw=1, ls='--', label='random')
plt.xlabel('False positive rate'); plt.ylabel('True positive rate')
plt.title('ROC curve   accuracy@0.5=%.3f' % acc)
plt.legend(loc='lower right', fontsize=8)

stages.title: Move the threshold, trade off the two errors
stages.note: Slide the decision threshold. Raising it makes the model more conservative about predicting 1: false positives fall but false negatives rise. Accuracy is one summary of that trade-off — and its best value is rarely exactly at 0.5.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: A dataset is 95% zeros. A model that predicts 0 for everyone reports 95% accuracy. What does that reveal?
choices: The model is excellent
Accuracy alone is misleading under class imbalance; check FN/TPR and AUC
Accuracy should always be replaced by pseudo-R²
The threshold must have been set above 0.95
stages.hint: How many true positives did that model catch?
stages.explain: It catches zero positives despite 95% accuracy, so accuracy is uninformative under imbalance — threshold-free measures like the ROC/AUC and the true-positive rate expose the failure.

stages.title: Check
choices: The model classifies everything perfectly
The model ranks positives above negatives no better than random chance
Exactly half the predictions are correct
The threshold is set to 0.5
stages.hint: AUC is the probability a random positive outscores a random negative.
stages.explain: AUC = 0.5 is the diagonal of the ROC plot — the model's probability ranking is no better than a coin flip, regardless of the chosen threshold.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Raising the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 will generally:
choices: Increase both false positives and false negatives
Decrease false positives but increase false negatives
Decrease both error types simultaneously
Leave the confusion matrix unchanged
stages.hint: A higher bar to predict '1' makes the model more cautious about positives.
stages.explain: Demanding p̂ ≥ 0.8 makes positive predictions rarer, so false positives fall while genuine positives get missed more often, raising false negatives — the classic precision/recall trade-off.

stages.title: Does 95% accuracy mean a good model?
stages.prompt: A dataset is 95% zeros. You just saw that always predicting 0 scores 95% accuracy. Claim: that 95% accuracy shows the classifier is performing well.
stages.hint: How many actual positives does the all-zeros rule catch? Think about the true-positive rate and the AUC, not raw accuracy.
stages.explain: This is the accuracy-under-imbalance trap. A model that predicts 0 for everyone catches ZERO positives yet still scores 95% — accuracy just echoes the base rate when classes are imbalanced. Judge such a model by threshold-free, ranking measures: the true-positive rate and the ROC AUC (0.5 = no better than chance here). Boundary: accuracy is informative only when the classes are roughly balanced and the costs of the two error types are similar; otherwise lean on AUC, precision/recall, or a cost-weighted threshold.
